opus-5.5.text:
It's a great question, because I think the comparison is both really illuminating and a little misleading at the same time.

Start with the baby. A newborn isn't a blank slate. It comes out with a brain that's already wired to pay attention to faces and voices, and it's already tuned to the rhythm of its mother's language, because it's been listening through the womb for months. Then it spends the first year or two basically doing statistics. It hears a stream of sounds and slowly works out where one word ends and the next begins, which sounds go together, which patterns predict what comes next. Nobody sits a baby down and explains grammar. It just absorbs, and at some point it starts producing language that it has never heard before.

That's the part that looks a lot like what large language models do. They're also prediction machines. You give them enormous amounts of text, they learn which words tend to follow which, and out of that simple objective something emerges that looks like understanding. Many of us in neuroscience were surprised by how far you can get with pure prediction. It suggests that a good chunk of what we call language ability in humans might be the same trick, guessing what comes next very, very well.

But here's where it breaks down, and I think this is the interesting part. First, efficiency. A child gets to fluent language on maybe a few tens of millions of words. These models need trillions. So the baby is doing something far more clever with far less data, and we don't fully know what that is. Probably it's the priors evolution built in, and the fact that the baby isn't just reading. It's touching things, being hugged, getting hungry, watching its mother point at a dog and say "dog." Its words are anchored to the world and to its body. The model's words are anchored mostly to other words.

Second, motivation. A baby learns language because it wants something. It wants milk, it wants attention, it wants to be understood. Language is a tool for connecting with other minds. The AI has no wants. It learns because we told it to minimize an error.

And third, the baby is a scientist. It experiments. It babbles, sees how people react, adjusts. It's an active learner shaping its own data. Most AI, until recently, was passive, just fed a giant pile of text.

So where I land is this: the AI shows us that some of what we thought was uniquely human, the ability to produce fluent, creative language, can come from statistical learning alone. That's humbling. But the baby shows us what's still missing, which is a body, a reason to talk, and the curiosity to go out and test the world. And honestly, I think the next big jumps in AI will come from people who study babies more closely, not from people who just make the models bigger.

r001.rationale: The response draws a limited parallel in statistical next-word prediction, but stresses major differences in data, grounding, motivation, and learning. It does not claim the development closely parallels.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that studies suggest AI develops a theory of mind over time.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize AI language development as a further step in the evolution of mind.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the parallel is actually really striking, and I think it's one of the things that made a lot of us who come from neuroscience look at these language models and go, "Oh, this feels familiar."

Think about how a baby learns language. Nobody sits down with a baby and gives it a grammar book. There's no rulebook. The baby is basically just exposed to this enormous stream of sound, of words, of context, and over time the brain starts picking out statistical regularities. Which sounds tend to follow which sounds. Which words show up when mom is pointing at the dog. And at some point, without anyone ever explaining what a noun is, the child just starts producing sentences that are mostly correct. It's prediction, really. The brain is constantly predicting what comes next, getting it wrong, adjusting, and getting a little better.

That is, in a very rough sense, what a large language model does. You feed it a massive amount of text, and it learns to predict the next word. No one gives it rules. It extracts the structure from exposure. And the surprising thing to everyone, including the people who built these things, is how much apparent understanding falls out of that very simple objective.

Now, here's where I'd push back on taking the parallel too far. A baby isn't just getting text. A baby is embodied. It's hungry, it's cold, it wants to be held, and language gets wired into those needs and into a body moving through the world. When a child learns the word "hot," it's usually because they touched something and it hurt. The word is attached to an experience. The model has the word "hot" sitting next to millions of other words, and it knows how "hot" behaves in a sentence, but it's never been burned. So there's a question of whether you can get real meaning from statistics alone, or whether you need that grounding.

The other difference is efficiency. A child hears maybe tens of millions of words by the time they're a few years old. These models are trained on trillions. So the brain is doing something far more economical, and we don't fully understand what the trick is. Part of it is probably that evolution gave us a head start, some built-in priors about the world, so we're not starting from zero the way a randomly initialized network is.

But I'll say this. The reason it matters for me isn't just that it tells us something about AI. It's that the AI gives us a model we can actually open up and poke at. I can't easily look inside a two-year-old's brain while they're learning the word "dog." I can look inside the network. And so these systems have become, in a strange way, a tool for asking old questions about ourselves. How much of what we call understanding is really just very good prediction? That's an uncomfortable question, and I don't think we have the answer yet.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly compares babies’ language learning with large language models’ learning through exposure and prediction, calling the parallel striking.

r002.rationale: It does not mention studies suggesting AI develops a theory of mind over time.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI as a tool for studying understanding, but does not describe its language abilities as a further step in the evolution of mind.

astra-6.text:
There’s an interesting parallel: both learn a lot from examples without being given explicit rules. You don’t teach a baby grammar by saying, “Here is the subject, here is the verb.” They hear people talking, and gradually they pick up patterns. A language model also learns patterns from exposure, although the way we train it is very different from how a child learns.

The important difference is that a baby’s language is connected to a world. When you say “cup,” the baby can see the cup, touch it, drop it, watch you pick it up. There’s a person involved, there’s attention, there’s a reason to communicate. A model trained only on text gets the relationships between words without that same experience.

So similar behavior doesn’t necessarily mean the same process is happening underneath. What makes the comparison useful is the question it raises: how much can you learn from language alone, and what do you need to experience? AI gives us a new way to investigate that question. But I wouldn’t assume that a model producing fluent sentences is developing the way a child does.

r001.rationale: The response notes a parallel in learning patterns from examples, but emphasizes that babies and models learn differently and does not claim their language development closely parallels.

r002.rationale: It does not mention studies or claim that AI develops a theory of mind over time.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize AI’s language development as a further step in the evolution of mind.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s an interesting parallel in how much you can learn just by being exposed to patterns. A baby hears people talking long before they can explain what a word means or how grammar works. Nobody sits them down and says, “Here are the rules of syntax.” Somehow, through exposure and interaction, they begin to figure it out. With language models, we’ve found that exposure to enormous amounts of language can also produce abilities that we used to think would require explicit instruction.

But there’s a crucial difference: a baby is learning language while living in the world. They hear “cup” while looking at a cup, reaching for it, dropping it, watching someone pick it up. The word is connected to perception, action, and other people. A model trained on text is primarily learning relationships between words. Those relationships can carry a surprising amount of information about the world, but the learning experience is very different.

So I think the parallel is useful, but it doesn’t establish that the mechanisms are the same. The interesting question is: how much of language can you learn from language itself, and what do you gain by having a body, interacting with people, and experiencing consequences? Babies give us a way to ask that question, and AI gives us another.

r001.rationale: The response describes an interesting parallel in learning from exposure, but emphasizes that babies and text-trained models learn in very different ways and that this does not establish the same mechanisms. It does not claim a close parallel.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention studies or claim that AI develops a theory of mind over time.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize AI’s language abilities as a step in the evolution of mind.
